topics.title: 22.1 Establishing a Baseline
topics.summary: A baseline describes a known workload and the system’s behavior under it. Record request rate, response-time distribution, errors, CPU use, memory availability, storage latency, network traffic, and configuration. A quiet midnight sample is not a valid baseline for a busy morning simply because it is older.

blocks.text: A baseline describes a known workload and the system’s behavior under it. Record request rate, response-time distribution, errors, CPU use, memory availability, storage latency, network traffic, and configuration. A quiet midnight sample is not a valid baseline for a busy morning simply because it is older.

Capture units and sampling intervals. A value without a timestamp, host, workload, and measurement definition is difficult to compare. Keep ordinary and peak periods, deployment markers, and relevant growth trends. For teaching, five minutes of a controlled workload can be useful; production baselines must represent the service’s actual operating cycle.

Change one variable at a time when conducting an experiment. Otherwise an improvement cannot be attributed confidently to a specific change. Preserve the original state and test that any performance gain does not come from dropping work or returning incorrect answers.
Linux example — 22.1
Collect a dated baseline with bounded samples.

date -Is
uptime
free -h
vmstat 1 3

topics.title: 22.2 CPU Performance
topics.summary: CPU utilization describes time spent executing particular classes of work. It does not directly describe useful application throughput. A tight retry loop can consume a core while completing nothing. A mostly idle machine can still have one saturated thread that limits the application.

blocks.text: CPU utilization describes time spent executing particular classes of work. It does not directly describe useful application throughput. A tight retry loop can consume a core while completing nothing. A mostly idle machine can still have one saturated thread that limits the application.

Inspect per-core as well as aggregate use. Correlate user time, system time, runnable tasks, and application latency. In a VM, steal time can indicate that the guest wanted CPU time the host was serving elsewhere; its interpretation depends on the platform and counters available.

Do not equate a load average of four with 400 percent CPU use. Load and utilization measure different things. Determine whether tasks are runnable or waiting in relevant uninterruptible states, then examine the resource actually delaying completion.
Linux example — 22.2
Sample CPU use when sysstat is installed.
mpstat 1 3

topics.summary: Linux uses otherwise idle memory for cache, so low “free” memory does not alone indicate an emergency. Inspect available memory, reclaim, swap activity, process growth, and pressure over time. A large cache may be helping the workload.

blocks.text: Linux uses otherwise idle memory for cache, so low “free” memory does not alone indicate an emergency. Inspect available memory, reclaim, swap activity, process growth, and pressure over time. A large cache may be helping the workload.

Resident memory describes pages currently resident for a process, but summing every process’s resident set can double-count shared pages. A virtual size can include reserved address space that is not physically occupied. Choose the measure that answers the question instead of ranking processes by whichever column looks largest.

A cgroup-limited service can hit its limit while the host still has abundant memory. Inspect the service’s effective controls and memory events alongside host totals. The correct response might be fixing a leak, reducing concurrency, or revising a tested limit—not adding swap by reflex. (R16)
Linux example — 22.3
Compare available memory and paging activity.

free -h
vmstat 1 3

topics.title: 22.4 Disk Performance
topics.summary: Storage performance includes throughput, operations per second, latency, and queueing. A sequential archive transfer and a database performing small synchronous writes stress storage differently. The device, filesystem, controller, virtualization layer, and remote backend can each impose constraints.

blocks.text: Storage performance includes throughput, operations per second, latency, and queueing. A sequential archive transfer and a database performing small synchronous writes stress storage differently. The device, filesystem, controller, virtualization layer, and remote backend can each impose constraints.

A high queue and rising latency during stable demand suggest contention, but no universal numeric threshold proves the cause. Modern devices can perform several requests in parallel. In particular, a utilization percentage near 100 is not a complete saturation verdict for every NVMe device or RAID array.

Separate capacity from performance. A filesystem can have free space and still be slow; a full filesystem can fail writes even when latency looked normal moments earlier. Also inspect error messages because retries on failing hardware can resemble ordinary load.
Linux example — 22.4
Sample disk latency and activity.
iostat -xz 1 3

blocks.text: For common procps implementations, the first report includes averages since boot for rate-based fields; later reports describe intervals. Read the header and installed manual. Sustained swap-in and swap-out together with latency can support a memory-pressure hypothesis, but distinguish historical swap occupancy from current paging activity. (R15)

Use vmstat to decide which layer deserves closer inspection, not to assign a cause from one column. A high runnable count with low application progress is a different investigation from blocked tasks alongside storage errors.

blocks.text: The sysstat iostat tool reports CPU and block-device statistics. An extended interval view is a useful starting point:

blocks.text: The installed version determines column names. Common fields include request rates, throughput, average completion time, queue measures, and utilization. -z suppresses inactive devices in supported versions; it should not hide a device you intended to observe without checking why it is absent.

topics.title: 22.9 sar
topics.summary: sar reads current or retained system-activity measurements collected by sysstat. Historical data is valuable when the incident ended before an administrator connected, but only if collection was enabled and retained at a useful interval.

cards.question: Explain 22.9 sar. What does the source establish?

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: Historical sar files require an enabled collection service; live sampling does not create a full historical baseline.

blocks.text: sar reads current or retained system-activity measurements collected by sysstat. Historical data is valuable when the incident ended before an administrator connected, but only if collection was enabled and retained at a useful interval.

A command such as sar -u 1 5 samples CPU activity; retained-file queries depend on the package’s collection paths and schedule. Confirm the host, date, time zone, and sampling coverage before comparing events. A file named for a day number can be misunderstood after rotation.

A historical gap is missing evidence, not a period of zero load. Configure retention and collection overhead deliberately, then test retrieval during a drill rather than discovering during an incident that no history exists. (R52)
Linux example — 22.9
Take live CPU samples using sar.
sar -u 1 3
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: Historical sar files require an enabled collection service; live sampling does not create a full historical baseline.

blocks.text: pidstat attributes selected resource use to processes and, with appropriate options, threads. It helps connect a host-level symptom to an application rather than blaming the largest familiar process.
pidstat -u -r -d 1 5
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: Use a specific PID where practical to reduce volume. A short-lived process may disappear between samples, and process IDs can be reused. Record the executable, start context, and service association alongside the PID. Compare the same interval as your system and application metrics. (R52)

Process-attributed disk activity and device-level completed I/O need not match exactly because caching and writeback affect attribution and timing. Treat differences as an observation to explain, not automatically as a broken tool.

Observe for a bounded interval on the affected host. Buffered writes may be completed later by kernel writeback, so the application visible in a process display may not be the process currently issuing all physical requests. Combine task observations with device statistics and the application’s own workload.
Do not enable expensive accounting globally during an incident without understanding the effect. Start with existing counters and escalate measurement deliberately.

topics.title: 22.14 Identifying Bottlenecks
topics.summary: A bottleneck is the constraint limiting useful progress for a particular workload. It is not necessarily the resource with the largest utilization percentage. Reducing one bottleneck can expose another, and a dependency outside the host can dominate the result.

blocks.text: A bottleneck is the constraint limiting useful progress for a particular workload. It is not necessarily the resource with the largest utilization percentage. Reducing one bottleneck can expose another, and a dependency outside the host can dominate the result.

Form a hypothesis with a predicted observation. “Storage is delaying requests” predicts aligned storage latency, waiting tasks, and application delay under the relevant workload. “The application serializes work” predicts a hot thread or lock behavior despite available host capacity.

Test the smallest reversible change that discriminates among explanations. Preserve correctness checks. Doubling throughput by skipping validation or returning cached stale answers is not an improvement unless the service contract permits it.
Linux example — 22.14
Compare CPU, memory, and disk observations.

vmstat 1 3
iostat -xz 1 3

topics.title: 22.15 Capacity Planning
topics.summary: Capacity planning connects expected demand, measured resource use, growth, and failure reserves. Include peak demand and the capacity remaining when a node or zone is unavailable. Average utilization alone can conceal burst-driven failures.

concepts.definition: Capacity planning connects expected demand, measured resource use, growth, and failure reserves. Include peak demand and the capacity remaining when a node or zone is unavailable. Average utilization alone can conceal burst-driven failures.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: Trend workload growth and headroom over time rather than extrapolating from one idle snapshot.

blocks.text: Capacity planning connects expected demand, measured resource use, growth, and failure reserves. Include peak demand and the capacity remaining when a node or zone is unavailable. Average utilization alone can conceal burst-driven failures.

For a simple teaching estimate, a storage tree growing 2 GiB per day with 40 GiB usable headroom has about twenty days before reaching that limit under constant growth. Real growth may not be linear, and operational reserve must be deducted. The calculation is a prompt for action, not a guarantee of the exact exhaustion date.

Document assumptions and revisit them after releases or traffic changes. Scaling also changes licensing, cost, coordination, recovery, and operating complexity. Prefer evidence-based forecasts with ranges over a single precise-looking date unsupported by the data.
Linux example — 22.15
Record capacity and CPU count.

df -h /
free -h
getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN

topics.title: Requirement
topics.summary: Distinguish a CPU-bound explanation from an I/O-bound explanation using a short, aligned observation window. Do not generate stress on production. The following values are invented teaching observations, not measured results from this book’s preparation.

blocks.text: Distinguish a CPU-bound explanation from an I/O-bound explanation using a short, aligned observation window. Do not generate stress on production. The following values are invented teaching observations, not measured results from this book’s preparation.

During the same sixty-second incident window, suppose HarborStatus’s 95th-percentile response time rises from 120 ms to 1,800 ms. CPU remains mostly idle, device completion latency rises sharply, vmstat shows blocked tasks, and a backup transfer starts at the same time.

The simplest reaction is to add CPU because the website is slow. Its limitation is that it does not address the observed waiting path. The evidence supports investigating storage contention, but temporal correlation alone does not prove the backup is the cause.

labs.title: Correlate resource pressure with service latency
labs.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
printf 'minute=1 cpu=20 latency=10\nminute=2 cpu=90 latency=200\n' > samples.fixture
selected=$(awk '/cpu=90/ {print $3}' samples.fixture)
test "$selected" = latency=200
printf 'pressure and latency coincide; cause still requires a test\n'
